column3: It repeats the exact claim that all dignity belongs to God while rejecting its pursuit through disbelieving allies.
It pairs good and evil deeds with differentiated return, supporting the focus's deed-consequence contrast.
It presents hostile plotting and God's overriding response, a close boundary for the focus's evil plotting clause.
Its distinction of evil from good and the losers' end supports the focus's opposed good-word and evil-plot structure.
The immediate context pairs righteous deeds with reward and disbelief with severe punishment.
Its non-failing commerce gives a direct economic counterpoint to the focus's statement that evil plotting fails.
It exactly repeats that all dignity belongs to God, adding consolation against hostile speech.
The preceding ayah contrasts an evil deed made attractive with God's knowledge, preparing the focus's judgment of evil plotting.
It has the broad motif of human plotting answered by God, but adds little after 8:30.
It attributes all plotting to God and directs the outcome toward the disbelievers, closely framing the focus's final clause.
The beautiful names connect only indirectly to the focus's good word and divine dignity.
It names kufr as exchange leading a people into the abode of ruin, a strong parallel to boor's failed outcome.
It distinguishes believers with righteous deeds from disbelievers under punishment, though in a broader return setting.
The local contrast of powerless invocation and informed report supports divine sovereignty but not the focus's main sequence.
It makes a requested righteous deed too late after death, sharpening that deeds, not merely words, matter.
It explicitly says evil plotting recoils upon its makers, the nearest local expansion of the focus's final assertion.
The local warning about Satan and the blazing fire supplies only the punishment background.
It names great plotting but lacks the focus's verdict that such plotting fails.
Its ascent image belongs to guidance and constriction, not the ascent of good speech.
God's being al-Aziz supports divine dignity only as a general attribute.
It calls a people boor after prolonged heedlessness, adding a communal instance of the focus's failed outcome.
It contrasts a coercive claim to honor with honor belonging to God, His messenger, and believers.
The local statement that none can withhold or release mercy besides God supports the sovereignty behind true dignity.
It joins warning and good news to believers who do righteous deeds, a secondary deed-and-reward parallel.
It distinguishes late verbal repentance from effective moral change, illuminating the focus's word-and-deed relation.
The local summons to remember divine provision establishes the sovereign source behind the focus's all-dignity claim.
It supplies the blessed return for believers who do righteous deeds, though it repeats an already established outcome.
It names the Lord of dignity and dissociates Him from false descriptions, but adds no ascent or deed relation.
Universal dominion and power are a broad basis for the focus's attribution of dignity to God.
It calls an evil expectation and its people boor, extending the failure motif to corrupted inward judgment.
The good/bad land contrast gives a figurative good-versus-evil productivity parallel, but is not about speech or plotting.
The local depiction of cosmic rule supports divine sovereignty but adds little beyond 35:2-3.
Its single ascent term offers only a remote lexical echo of the focus's upward movement.
It gives evil deeds their matching recompense and humiliation, clarifying the focus's warning of severe punishment.
The immediately preceding assurance about earlier rejected messengers supplies the adversarial setting for the focus.
Raised couches do not materially clarify dignity, ascent, righteous deeds, or evil plotting.
It joins a demand for privileged revelation, humiliation, severe punishment, and plotting by criminals.
It challenges a group's privileged claim through punishment and universal dominion, a distant dignity boundary.
Its ascent is a retreat in battle and does not illuminate the focus's ascent of good speech.
Forgiveness, repentance, severe punishment, and return provide only a general judgment frame.
The local creation and angelic messengers establish power and increase, but not the focus's word-deed sequence.
It states that God establishes truth through His words despite criminals, a useful counterpart to failed evil plotting.
Protection from evil deeds and attainment of success is a general consequence parallel.
The raised roof has no meaningful relation to the focus's theological ascent.
Messengers as warners remove excuse, with only a broad connection to accountability and divine might.
It depicts sinful pride and its hellish end, a pointed counterexample to the focus's proper source of dignity.
The local contrast of two seas and provision supports good/evil differentiation but not the core verbal-action sequence.
It directly combines wholesome provision, righteous action, and divine knowledge of what is done.
It declares opposition after response to God futile and liable to severe punishment, close to the failure of evil schemes.
The immediate wind-and-revival image supplies the local upward and life-giving movement surrounding the focus.
It makes improper speech toward the Prophet able to nullify deeds, strongly linking speech with the standing of action.
It contrasts those who answer their Lord with those facing an evil reckoning, supporting response and consequence.
It joins repentance, faith, and righteous work with the conversion of evil deeds into good, a useful transformation counterpart.
Divine strength and dignity accompany rescue, but this adds little to the already established dignity theme.
It says elite criminals plot only against themselves, closely supporting the self-defeating scheme motif.
God raising Jesus to Himself is a distinct ascent scene, only broadly resonant with the focus's upward language.
It calls a false utterance great and emerging from mouths, a contrast boundary for the focus's good word.
It distinguishes evil from good and makes faith and reverence consequential, though without the speech motif.
The people are made harvested and extinguished, a vivid consequence for failed opposition but already indirect.
It explicitly joins repentance with righteous work and return to God, reinforcing action as realized return.
It explicitly guides people to good speech and to the praised path, a close parallel to the focus's good word.
God's divinity in heaven and earth supports universal sovereignty but is redundant for dignity.
The good land and commanded gratitude offer only a distant good/productivity resonance.
It recounts a past conspiracy within a revelation narrative, without the focus's judgment on plotting.
It links denial with a prepared blaze, a compact punishment parallel to the focus's severe punishment.
Faith, righteous work, good recompense, and gentle command repeat the established deed-reward pattern.
It rejects treating evil-doers as equal to believers who do righteous deeds, sharpening the focus's moral division.
Raised bedding does not add a meaningful connection to the focus's ascent or dignity.
It describes sharp speech, unbelief, and works rendered futile, a negative speech-action counterpart.
The consolation against their plotting repeats the adversarial setting without a new outcome.
Lowering and raising provide only an abstract polarity, not the focus's ascent of good speech.
It states that association nullifies works and makes one a loser, an action-failure counterpart.
It concerns false hearing, distortion of words, and punishment, but is too diffuse after stronger speech-action parallels.
God's high ranks and descent of the spirit give a broad vertical image, not the focus's ascending word.
The uninterrupted reward for righteous deeds repeats the established positive outcome with little added detail.
Advice failing under divine misguidance is only a remote verbal-response boundary.
Universal dominion and power repeat the sovereign foundation without clarifying the focus's sequence.
It combines faith, righteous deeds, truth-bearing mutual counsel, and patience, giving a compact communal word-and-deed parallel.
God's ownership of the first and last is too general to add to the dignity claim.
The exchange of bad for good in orphan property is a distinct ethical setting, with only a loose contrast.
Its distribution rule and obedience to the messenger concern circulation and command, not the focus's central relation.
Righteous deeds and gardens repeat the reward pattern without a speech, dignity, or plotting dimension.
Praise of God as Lord of the worlds does not materially clarify the focus beyond general divine exaltation.
Good dwellings and great success follow a different promise sequence and add little after earlier deed-reward cards.
God's conclusive proof and universal guidance provide only a broad authority backdrop.
It makes a good word a sound tree whose branch is in heaven, the closest image of the focus's good word ascending.
It repeats consolation against their plotting, already covered by 8:30 and 27:70.
The closing assertion that God is strong and mighty is a general dignity parallel only.
It mentions people long engaged in evil deeds but not their plot's failure or the good-word relation.
Its false self-assurance and punishment form a broad evil-deed consequence, but the contrast route is not positive support.
Its creator-and-idol polemic supports exclusive sovereignty but is too general at this late rank.
A prior word and appointed term explain delayed consequence, a secondary temporal context for punishment.
Witness-bearing and testing obedience offer a distant link to faithful action, not the focus's terms.
Divine knowledge of deeds provides an accountability backdrop without speech, dignity, or plotting.
The presentation of every good and evil deed is a broad accountability parallel already well covered.
The plea for rescue from a people's deeds supplies only a remote boundary against evil action.
Household eating permissions and greeting etiquette do not clarify the focus's themes.
Disavowal of others' deeds is a limited moral boundary, not a direct word-deed or plotting relation.
Its regulated private speech and divine knowledge belong to a legal setting unrelated to the focus's ascent.
Guidance and inner rectification are a general positive outcome, with no direct dignity, word, or plotting link.
It makes honor and abasement God's direct acts within His sovereignty, supplying a major omitted parallel to the focus's source of dignity.
It assures believers that hostile plotting will not harm them under reverence, adding a practical counterpart to the scheme's failure.
It explicitly states that God weakens the disbelievers' plot, a direct omitted parallel to the final clause.
The good tree continually bears fruit by its Lord's permission, extending the productive outcome of the good word in 14:24.
The evil word is likened to an uprooted bad tree with no stability, a close counterimage to the focus's failed evil plotting.
Those who plot evil are warned against security from God's overturning action, adding a distinct consequence scene.
Faith and righteous action lead to good life and better recompense, a compact realization of the focus's deed theme.
The command to speak what is best sets a practical counterpart to the focus's good word and its vulnerability to Satanic discord.
It rejects any protector from humiliation and commands God's magnification, closely bounding the focus's account of true dignity.
It joins righteous action with unalloyed worship, clarifying the action appropriate to ascent toward God.
The believer who comes with righteous deeds receives the highest ranks, linking deeds with upward elevation.
Repentance, faith, and righteous action are named as the path to forgiveness, extending the focus's positive action sequence.
Belief and righteous deeds receive divine establishment, a social outcome complementary to the focus's dignity claim.
The servants of the Merciful answer ignorance with peace, giving a concrete ethical form to good speech.
Faith and righteous deeds erase evil deeds and bring the best recompense, sharpening the good-evil reversal.
Recitation, prayer, and the prohibition of indecency and evil connect divine remembrance with action against evil.
The command to speak a sound word is a direct omitted counterpart to the focus's good word.
It immediately states that sound speech brings rectification of deeds, the closest explicit word-deed linkage omitted from the list.
It denies that wealth and children confer nearness except through faith and righteous deeds, refining the focus's account of true dignity.
It identifies all people as dependent on God while He is self-sufficient and praiseworthy, a key local foundation for dignity belonging wholly to Him.
It promises full reward and increase to those who recite the Book, pray, and spend, extending the local productive-action sequence.
It joins the best speech with calling to God and doing righteous work, an especially close omitted parallel to 35:10.
Repelling evil with what is better gives a concrete ethical contrast to evil plotting.
Whoever acts righteously benefits himself and whoever acts evilly bears it, then all return to God; this clarifies the focus's moral consequence.
Faith, righteous deeds, belief in revelation, and rectification are explicitly joined, strongly extending the focus's action theme.
It states that disbelievers plot while they themselves are the ones caught by plotting, a direct omitted parallel to the plot's failure.
It rebukes saying what one does not do, providing a sharp negative boundary for the focus's coordination of word and righteous deed.
It names their plotting before the immediate divine counter-plot, a concise direct counterpart to 35:10's evil plotting.
